title: CAP Theorem
subtitle: Define read and write behavior when replicas cannot communicate
objectives: State CAP precisely, and explain why 'pick two of three' is a misleading slogan
Explain why partition tolerance isn't optional and what the real choice is
Work out what CP and AP actually feel like for a user
Apply the real-world version: the tradeoff exists even when the network is healthy

exercises.title: A network partition prevents replicas from exchanging updates
exercises.body: A network partition occurs when nodes remain running but messages between groups cannot be delivered. If datacenter A accepts a write, datacenter B cannot observe it until communication recovers. A request at B must use local state, wait, or fail because B cannot verify freshness.
exercises.note: Serving from both groups preserves availability and permits stale or conflicting state. Refusing service in one group preserves consistency and reduces availability.

exercises.prompt: A network partition separates two replicas. Stop writes on the isolated replica to prevent two conflicting account balances.
exercises.beforeStatus: PARTITION RESULT · A accepts $100; B accepts $70 · balances conflict
exercises.afterStatus: PARTITION RESULT · A accepts writes; B returns unavailable for writes
exercises.result: Consistency was preserved by sacrificing write availability
exercises.why: During a partition, refusing writes on the side without authority prevents divergent committed balances, preserving consistency while reducing availability. Reads or writes that can tolerate conflict may make a different choice.

exercises.prompt: A network partition isolates Replica B. Place the two replicas, connect their replication link, and show that the link is broken while Replica B rejects writes.
exercises.why: A partition is a failed communication link between replicas, not a component that processes traffic. Replica B rejects writes because it cannot prove that it still has authority; allowing both sides to commit could create conflicting balances.

exercises.prompt: Two datacenters hold copies of your data. The network link between them fails, but both are alive and users are hitting both. A user writes to datacenter A. What can datacenter B do about it?
choices: Nothing — it cannot hear about the write, so it must either serve data it knows might be stale, or refuse to answer
exercises.why: While the link is down, B cannot learn whether A accepted a newer write. B must either answer from potentially stale local state, preserving availability, or refuse until it can verify the latest state, preserving consistency.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter of CAP to what it means.

pairs.right: Every read sees the most recent write
Every request gets a non-error response
The system keeps working when the network splits
Nodes alive, but unable to reach each other

exercises.why: In the CAP theorem, consistency means every successful read reflects the latest completed write, availability means every request to a nonfailed node receives a response, and partition tolerance means operation continues despite lost messages between node groups.

exercises.prompt: CAP is usually taught as 'pick two of three'. Why is that misleading?
choices: Because you can actually have all three
Because partitions aren't a design choice — networks fail whether you like it or not, so P isn't something you can decline
Because there are really four properties
Because it only applies to NoSQL
exercises.why: A distributed system cannot prevent network partitions. During a partition, nodes cannot both guarantee the latest value and respond independently, so the required choice is between consistency and availability for that failure interval.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'CA' not a valid guarantee for a distributed service during a partition?
choices: Because consistency and availability cannot coexist on any distributed system
Because once required communication fails, the service must either reject some requests or let isolated nodes answer without verified-fresh state
Because a partition always crashes every replica
exercises.why: A distributed service can provide consistency and availability while required nodes can communicate. Once a partition prevents that communication, an isolated node cannot both verify the latest completed write and guarantee a response, so the service must sacrifice consistency or availability for affected operations.

exercises.prompt: Datacenter A accepted value 8. Build the AP path when B remains available across a broken link.
exercises.why: The partitioned link prevents B from learning A's accepted value 8, so an availability-preserving B answers from its local copy and returns 7. That keeps the request successful, but the user acts on stale state; a consistency-preserving path would instead reject or wait until it could establish authority.

exercises.prompt: During a partition, why can't a node just tell whether it's the one that's cut off?
choices: It can — it checks its network card
It can't: from inside, 'the other node is dead', 'the other node is slow', and 'I am the one who's isolated' all look identical
exercises.why: A node observes only missing or delayed messages. That evidence cannot distinguish a failed peer, a slow peer, packet loss, or isolation of the observing node, so neither side can identify itself as the disconnected side from silence alone.

exercises.title: A CP system rejects operations that cannot prove a consistent state
exercises.body: A consistency-and-partition-tolerant (CP) system requires an operation to reach a quorum or authoritative leader before it succeeds. During a partition, a group lacking that authority rejects or blocks reads and writes, preventing it from serving potentially stale state.
exercises.note: In a majority-quorum configuration, authority requires more than half of configured voters. Other quorum schemes must preserve the required intersection between authoritative sets.

exercises.prompt: A partition splits your cluster. You choose consistency. What does a user on the minority side experience?
choices: Errors or timeouts — the system refuses to serve rather than risk answering with data it can't verify
Their writes queue up and apply later
exercises.why: A consistency-preserving node must reject a request when it cannot confirm that its state includes the latest committed write. Users on the non-quorate side therefore receive errors or timeouts until communication or quorum is restored.

exercises.prompt: How does a CP system decide which side of a partition may keep serving?
choices: A quorum — the side holding a majority of nodes can proceed, and the minority steps back, because only one side can hold a majority
The side with the newest data
exercises.why: Any two majorities of the same membership overlap, so disjoint partition sides cannot both obtain a quorum. Odd cluster sizes use nodes efficiently: three and four nodes both tolerate only one unavailable node when a majority is required.

exercises.prompt: A CP cluster has 5 configured voters and needs 3 votes. Place the write behavior on each side of a 3–2 partition.
exercises.why: Side A can gather the required three votes and continue committing writes, while side B has only two and must reject them even though both nodes are healthy. If the minority also accepted writes, the two sides could create conflicting histories and the CP safety guarantee would be lost.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: A CP cluster has 5 configured voters and needs 3 votes. Place the write behavior on each side of a 3–2 partition.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Partition Side A → Accept writes: quorum 3/5; Partition Side B → Reject writes: only 2/5. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Side A can gather the required three votes and continue committing writes, while side B has only two and must reject them even though both nodes are healthy. If the minority also accepted writes, the two sides could create conflicting histories and the CP safety guarantee would be lost.

exercises.prompt: Which systems should lean CP? Select all.
choices: A view counter on a video
exercises.why: Balances, inventory, and locks create commitments based on the returned value. A stale answer can permit double spending, overselling, or concurrent ownership, so rejecting requests during a partition is safer than accepting inconsistent operations.

exercises.prompt: A distributed lock service goes AP — both sides of a partition keep granting locks. What breaks?
choices: Two clients hold 'the same' lock simultaneously, which destroys the only property a lock exists to provide
exercises.why: Mutual exclusion requires at most one valid lock holder. If both partition sides grant the same lock, protected clients can modify the resource concurrently, violating the lock's safety property; the non-quorate side must stop granting locks.

exercises.prompt: What's the real cost of choosing CP?
choices: Downtime for anyone who can't reach a quorum — you've converted a network problem into a visible outage, on purpose
exercises.why: Consistency during a partition is maintained by refusing operations that cannot be verified through a quorum. This produces a partial outage for affected users, exchanging service availability for prevention of stale reads and conflicting writes.

exercises.title: An AP system serves requests from replicas that may diverge
exercises.body: An availability-and-partition-tolerant (AP) system lets each reachable replica accept operations during a partition. Each side returns its local value and records local writes. When communication recovers, replicas exchange versions and reconcile concurrent changes.
exercises.note: Reconciliation must match the data's semantics. Last-write-wins can discard a valid update when clocks disagree or users edit concurrently.

exercises.prompt: Same partition, but you choose availability. What does the user on the minority side experience?
choices: A normal response — served from that node's own copy, which may be missing writes that happened on the other side
exercises.why: An availability-preserving node responds from its reachable local state even when that state may be stale. Users continue receiving responses, while writes or updates accepted on the other side may remain invisible until replication resumes.

exercises.prompt: Both sides accepted concurrent profile edits during an AP partition. Build the recovery path that makes replicas converge after the link heals.
exercises.why: After replicas exchange versions, conflict detection identifies the concurrent edits and a deterministic domain rule selects or merges one result that both replicas apply. If nodes resolve the same conflict differently, they remain divergent; a last-write-wins rule converges but can silently discard a valid edit when clocks or user intent disagree.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Both sides accepted concurrent profile edits during an AP partition. Build the recovery path that makes replicas converge after the link heals.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Replica A → Conflict Detection; Replica B → Conflict Detection; Conflict Detection → Deterministic Resolution; Deterministic Resolution → Converged Replicas. That topology is the evidence for the answer: After replicas exchange versions, conflict detection identifies the concurrent edits and a deterministic domain rule selects or merges one result that both replicas apply. If nodes resolve the same conflict differently, they remain divergent; a last-write-wins rule converges but can silently discard a valid edit when clocks or user intent disagree.

exercises.prompt: Match each conflict resolution strategy.

pairs.right: Simple — and silently destroys one edit
Push the choice to the user or app

exercises.why: Conflict rules depend on the operation's semantics. A conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) guarantees convergence when replicas apply its defined merge rules, but a converged result can still violate an application rule such as an inventory limit. Last-write-wins instead selects one replacement value and may discard another valid edit.

exercises.prompt: Why is a shopping cart the classic AP example?
choices: Amazon reasoned that a customer being unable to add to cart is a lost sale, while a rare merge oddity is a recoverable annoyance — availability was worth more than perfect consistency
exercises.why: Keeping cart additions available preserves shopping activity during a partition, and cart conflicts can be reviewed or corrected before checkout. Payment and inventory commits require stricter coordination because an inconsistent result creates a financial obligation.

exercises.prompt: Which systems reasonably lean AP? Select all.
choices: An account balance shown before a transfer
exercises.why: Feeds, Domain Name System records, and like counts can remain useful while replicas temporarily return older values. A stale account balance can cause a user or service to authorize an invalid transfer, so its inconsistency has a higher operational cost.

exercises.prompt: What's the real cost of choosing AP?
choices: Some users act on stale data, and after the partition heals you own a reconciliation problem that no library can decide for you
Nothing — AP is strictly better for user experience
exercises.why: Availability during a partition permits replicas to diverge. When communication returns, the system must detect and reconcile concurrent values, and its predefined merge rule may discard, combine, or surface conflicting updates.

exercises.title: Linearizable consistency requires coordination even without a partition
exercises.body: CAP constrains behavior during a partition. With a healthy network, an operation that must establish freshness or commitment coordinates with protocol authority. A write may wait for a quorum; a read may use the leader, a valid lease, or a read quorum, depending on the protocol.
exercises.note: Coordination cost depends on the operation and protocol. A stale follower read may avoid a round trip, while a cross-region quorum write waits for distant acknowledgements.

exercises.prompt: Your network is healthy — no partition at all. Does CAP say anything about your system right now?
choices: Yes — you must still pick two
No — CAP only constrains you DURING a partition. With a healthy network you can have both consistency and availability
exercises.why: The CAP theorem constrains behavior only while a network partition prevents required communication. With healthy connectivity, a system may provide both consistent results and successful responses, subject to its normal protocol and capacity.

exercises.prompt: So if CAP is silent when the network is fine, what tradeoff still exists during normal operation?
choices: Latency versus consistency: operations that must establish freshness or commitment may wait for protocol authority, while permitted stale reads can avoid that work
exercises.why: When the network is healthy, a quorum write must gather acknowledgements and some reads must confirm authority or freshness. A leader or valid lease can serve other linearizable reads without a fresh quorum round trip, while a permitted stale follower read can reduce latency further. PACELC describes this normal-case latency-versus-consistency choice.

exercises.prompt: Why does that latency-vs-consistency tradeoff matter more day to day than CAP itself?
choices: Because partitions may be rare while freshness-sensitive reads and committed writes pay their protocol's coordination cost during normal traffic
Because latency is easier to measure
exercises.why: Partition policy is exercised during link failure, while normal traffic repeatedly pays whatever its chosen read and write paths require. Quorum writes wait for enough replicas, leader or lease reads can avoid a fresh quorum, and follower reads are faster only when the contract permits staleness.

exercises.prompt: You're designing 'number of people currently viewing this page'. A partition splits your cluster. Slide toward your choice.
exercises.leftLabel: CP — refuse rather than show a wrong count
exercises.why: A viewer count can remain useful when briefly stale because it does not authorize an irreversible action. Serving local counts preserves the feature during a partition, and replicas can reconcile their values after communication resumes.

exercises.prompt: A vendor says their database is 'CA — no compromises'. What should you conclude?
choices: The claim omits the failure condition: if the service is distributed, ask which operations reject or may return stale data when required communication fails
It's the right choice for everything
exercises.why: A distributed database must have defined behavior when replicas cannot communicate. The meaningful evaluation is whether each partition side serves reads or writes, rejects them, or serves potentially stale data under that condition.

exercises.prompt: Should one system pick CP or AP for all its data?
choices: No — different data has different costs of being wrong, so the same product can be CP for payments and AP for the activity feed
Yes — the database decides for you
exercises.why: CAP behavior can differ by operation and dataset. A system may require quorum writes for balances while serving feeds from local replicas because the consequences of conflicting financial commits and stale feed entries differ.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of CAP?
choices: During a partition you must choose between refusing to answer and risking a stale answer — and the rest of the time, the live tradeoff is consistency against latency
exercises.why: During a partition, a distributed operation must sacrifice consistency or availability because required messages cannot cross the split. PACELC extends the analysis to healthy periods, when coordination for consistency is traded against lower latency.

exercises.prompt: Two warehouse regions lose connectivity. The last robot part must never be allocated twice. What should the isolated side without authority do?
choices: Allocate locally and hope reconciliation works
exercises.why: The invariant forbids conflicting allocations. During the partition, a side unable to establish authoritative state sacrifices availability for that operation rather than creating two winners.
